### GRI 302 Energy  
Unilever’s total energy consumption in 2025 was 5,224 thousand MWh, a decrease from 6,482 thousand MWh in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Renewable energy accounted for 62% of total energy consumption in 2025 (59% in 2024), with fossil sources comprising 38% (41% in 2024) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Purchased or acquired electricity, heat, steam and cooling from renewable sources totalled 1,674 thousand MWh in 2025, while self-generated non-fuel renewable energy amounted to 47 thousand MWh [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Unilever sourced 88% of its electricity from renewable sources in 2025 (85% in 2024), primarily through unbundled RECs (63%), purchased renewable electricity (85%), and off-site Power Purchase Agreements (13%) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_64]. Energy intensity—measured as MWh per € million net revenue—was 103 in 2025, down from 107 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_64].

### GRI 303 Water  
Total water consumption across Unilever’s own operations was 14 million m³ in 2025, down from 17 million m³ in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Of this, 9 million m³ was consumed in areas at high or extremely high water stress (ESRS definition), and 10 million m³ under Unilever’s broader definition incorporating site-specific risk assessments [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Water recycled and reused totalled 2 million m³ in both 2025 and 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Water intensity—water consumption per € million turnover—was 272 m³/€ million in 2025, compared to 281 m³/€ million in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Unilever does not set formal global targets for water withdrawal in its own operations or upstream value chain; instead, it manages water risk through local environmental performance targets and the Responsible Sourcing Policy (RPP) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_73]. Its voluntary target is to implement water stewardship programmes in 100 locations in water-stressed areas by 2030; 29 such programmes were active in 2025 (21 in 2024) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_74].

### GRI 305 Emissions  
Unilever’s total Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions (market-based) were 0.54 MtCO₂e in 2025 (0.47 MtCO₂e in 2024), representing a 77% reduction against the 2015 baseline [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_49]. Total Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG emissions (market-based) were 97.04 MtCO₂e in 2025, down 11% from 108.65 MtCO₂e in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_58]. Scope 3 emissions in scope of Unilever’s net zero ambition totalled 47.21 MtCO₂e in 2025 (56.61 MtCO₂e in 2024), with Purchased Goods and Services accounting for 37.91 MtCO₂e [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_58]. The company reported an overall 5% decrease in total Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions in 2025 versus 2024 (including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60]. Unilever’s near-term climate targets—validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)—include a 100% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 (vs. 2015 baseline) and a 42% reduction in Scope 3 Energy & Industrial (E&I) emissions by 2030 (vs. 2021 baseline) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_25][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_48].

### GRI 306 Waste  
Total waste generated in Unilever’s own operations was 493 thousand tonnes in 2025, down from 731 thousand tonnes in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Of this, 467 thousand tonnes of non-hazardous waste and 19 thousand tonnes of hazardous waste were diverted from disposal [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Non-recycled waste totalled 114 thousand tonnes (23% of total waste), down from 183 thousand tonnes (25%) in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Hazardous waste directed to disposal was 5 thousand tonnes (4 thousand tonnes via incineration without energy recovery; 1 thousand tonnes via landfilling), while non-hazardous waste directed to disposal was 2 thousand tonnes (all via landfilling) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Unilever’s Climate Transition Action Plan (CTAP), approved by shareholders in 2024, outlines its 2030 climate targets and integrates mitigation, adaptation and advocacy actions into its three-year strategic planning cycle [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_25]. The CTAP supports Unilever’s long-term net zero ambition by 2039 and includes scenario analysis aligned with IPCC SSP pathways (<2°C, <3°C, >4°C) and TNFD-aligned nature scenarios (High Nature Preservation, Delayed Nature Action, High Nature Degradation) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_30]. Climate-related risks—including systemic biodiversity collapse, supply chain disruption from ecosystem degradation, and regulatory exposure from Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes—are embedded in enterprise risk management and reviewed annually [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_20][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_15]. Metrics include absolute GHG emissions (Scope 1–3), energy mix, water consumption in stressed basins, and waste diversion rates—all reported annually against science-based and voluntary targets [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_47][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_74].

### Not covered in source material  
- Detailed breakdown of water consumption by facility type (manufacturing vs. logistics vs. office) beyond aggregate figures.  
- Quantitative data on wastewater discharge volumes or quality parameters (e.g., BOD, COD).  
- Scope 3 Category 11 (Consumer Use of Sold Products) emissions disaggregated by product category or geography beyond the 13-country representative sample methodology.  
- Specific metrics or progress on circular economy initiatives beyond packaging recyclability (e.g., reuse systems, refill infrastructure uptake).  
- GHG removals or carbon sequestration activities within Unilever’s operational boundary (e.g., on-site afforestation, soil carbon projects).

### Occupational Health & Safety  
Unilever reported a Total Recordable Frequency Rate (TRFR) of 0.41 recordable work-related accidents per 1 million hours worked in 2025, down from 0.55 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. This metric covers both employees and non-employees (e.g., contractors), with employee-specific TRFR decreasing from 0.58 to 0.43 over the same period [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. The number of work-related accidents declined to 92 in 2025 (84 involving employees, 8 involving non-employees), compared to 165 in 2024 (152 and 13, respectively) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. Days lost due to injuries, fatalities, and work-related ill health totalled 1,936 in 2025, a reduction from 2,946 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. Notably, one fatality occurred in 2025 within the demerged Ice Cream business — a contractor who died due to workplace violence at an Ice Cream factory; Unilever conducted a full investigation and applied lessons globally [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_137]. All Unilever employees were covered by the company’s health and safety management system in both 2025 and 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. Work-related ill health incidents were reported as two in 2025, while no figure was disclosed for 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136].

### Training  
Unilever delivered mandatory annual Code of Business Principles (COBP) training to all employees in 2025, including content on recognising bullying and harassment and discrimination [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Additional mandatory training — such as sexual harassment training — was implemented in several countries to meet regulatory requirements [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Targeted capability-building initiatives included global AI training covering prompt engineering, responsible AI use, and practical applications (e.g., AI-powered menu suggestions, Copilot for financial reporting) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Social-First training was also provided globally to marketers on applying cultural principles across insight generation, growth strategy, and brand building [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Training on forced labour recognition, working hours policy, and inclusion was delivered via cross-function ‘learning hours’ and the Workday global learning platform [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. These efforts align with Unilever’s broader People Strategy, which prioritises talent development and organisational effectiveness through upskilling and streamlined learning platforms [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_126][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127].

### Diversity  
At the top management level (Unilever Leadership Executive and senior management one level below), women constituted 29% (27 individuals) of the 92-strong cohort in 2025, down from 32% (35 of 109) in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133]. Across the total workforce, women represented 37% (35,762 of 96,092) of employees at year-end 2025, compared to 37% (44,313 of 120,040) in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_131]. Age distribution showed 18% of employees under 30, 66% aged 30–50, and 16% over 50 in 2025 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133]. The gender pay gap is disclosed in the remuneration metrics section, though the specific value is not provided in the source material [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_137].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
Unilever requires business partners to adhere to the Responsible Partner Policy (RPP), which mandates human rights compliance, remediation of negative impacts, and alignment with ILO Conventions and UNGPs [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Suppliers of in-scope materials must comply with the People & Nature Policy, which requires human rights due diligence across their operations and supply chains, independent verification, and embedding of RPP standards [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Business partners confirm compliance annually via self-assessments, due diligence, and risk-based audits; outcomes determine approval status and inform risk-tiering based on geography and service type [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Supply chain mapping and country- and commodity-level risk analysis support targeted verification, including desktop and on-the-ground audits where risks are elevated [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_116]. When issues arise, Unilever engages partners to implement corrective actions; persistent non-compliance may lead to disengagement guided by internal human rights impact assessments [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_116].

### Governance Oversight and Accountability

Unilever’s Board holds ultimate accountability for the management of all material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs), including sustainability-related matters, and delegates day-to-day oversight to the Unilever Leadership Executive (ULE) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7]. The Board’s governance structure is supported by four key subcommittees: the Corporate Responsibility Committee (CRC), Audit Committee, Remuneration Committee, and Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee — each with defined terms of reference published on Unilever’s website [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7]. The CRC reviews the sustainability strategy, tracks progress against goals, and assesses reputational impacts of material IROs, receiving updates from the global Sustainability function five times per year [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7]. The Audit Committee oversees risk management processes—including the double materiality assessment (DMA)—non-financial disclosures (including under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, ESRS), and assurance over sustainability reporting [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7]. The Remuneration Committee aligns the long-term Performance Share Plan (PSP) with sustainability performance, assigning 15% weight to the Sustainability Progress Index (SPI) in PSP awards for 2025 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_8][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_9]. The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee ensures Board composition includes members with relevant sustainability expertise [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7].

### Anti-Corruption and Business Integrity Framework

Unilever maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, as codified in its Code of Business Principles (COBP) and supporting Code Policies, which prohibit public and commercial bribery—including facilitation payments—regardless of financial value [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_164]. These policies apply to all employees and extend to business partners through the Responsible Partner Policy (RPP), which mandates adherence to Unilever’s anti-corruption standards across the value chain [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_164][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_161]. In 2025, Unilever conducted periodic bespoke anti-corruption and anti-bribery risk assessments to identify high-risk geographies and business activities, informing tailored mitigation measures and targeted training [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_164]. All employees completed mandatory annual anti-corruption and anti-bribery training; Board members also received dedicated training, sponsored by the Chief Legal Officer and Chief Business Integrity Officer and overseen by the CRC [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165]. No incidents of corruption or bribery resulting in convictions or fines occurred for Unilever Group companies in 2025, nor were there deferred prosecution agreements or other significant enforcement actions related to anti-corruption breaches that year [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165].

### Sustainability Integration into Strategy and Risk Management

In 2024, the ULE approved a refocused sustainability strategy anchored by 15 externally facing goals across climate, nature, plastics, and livelihoods—each assigned to a ULE member with clear mitigation plans and timelines [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_8]. A re-established Executive-level Sustainability Steering Committee meets monthly to review progress and resolve delivery issues, while the ULE receives periodic updates [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_8]. Sustainability due diligence is embedded across governance, strategy, and business model via the DMA, which informs identification and assessment of material IROs—including governance-related risks such as business conduct and anti-bribery compliance [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_156][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_9]. The 2025 DMA identified “Business Conduct” and “Anti-bribery and corruption” as material risks, citing potential reputational damage and legal/financial consequences from ethical failures or non-compliance [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_156][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_157]. Oversight of sustainability reporting integrity rests with the Group Controller, who manages risks related to data completeness, accuracy, and availability; for each ESRS topic, a ULE Sponsor and designated Sustainability and Business owners are appointed [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_9].

### Political Engagement and Supplier Governance

Unilever engages in advocacy and lobbying—directly and indirectly through trade associations—to advance policy in climate, nature, plastics, and livelihoods, always aligned with its Code and Code Policies requiring honesty, integrity, openness, and compliance with applicable laws [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165]. Oversight of national government engagement and lobbying activity in 2025 was led by the Chief Corporate Affairs and Communications Officer [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165]. Supplier relationships are governed by the Responsible Sourcing and Business Partnering Code Policy, mandating fair treatment and requiring third parties to uphold Unilever’s standards—including anti-corruption requirements—through onboarding, contracting, and ongoing monitoring [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_161]. The RPP applies beyond Tier 1 suppliers, expecting cascading of equivalent requirements into their supply chains [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_161].

### Not covered in source material

The provided context does not disclose: (1) specific composition details of the Board or committees (e.g., number of independent directors, gender balance figures); (2) quantitative metrics on whistleblower reports, investigations, or resolution timelines; (3) board-level climate or nature risk oversight beyond committee mandates; (4) TCFD-aligned governance disclosures on climate risk integration into board agendas or director expertise; (5) verification or assurance provider details for anti-corruption disclosures; (6) executive remuneration targets beyond the 15% SPI weighting; (7) board evaluation outcomes related to sustainability competence.

### GRI 302 Energy  
Unilever’s total energy consumption in 2025 was 5,224 thousand MWh, down from 6,482 thousand MWh in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Renewable sources accounted for 62% of total energy consumption in 2025 (59% in 2024), while fossil sources comprised 38% (41% in 2024) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Consumption of purchased or acquired electricity, heat, steam and cooling from renewable sources totalled 1,674 thousand MWh in 2025; self-generated non-fuel renewable energy amounted to 47 thousand MWh [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Unilever sourced 88% of its electricity from renewable sources in 2025 (85% in 2024), composed of: purchased renewable electricity (85% of electricity supply), on-site Purchase Power Agreements (1% in 2025), off-site PPAs (13%), green tariffs/bundled RECs (8%), and unbundled RECs (63%) — with these categories representing overlapping coverage mechanisms under the market-based method, not mutually exclusive shares of total supply [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_64]. Energy intensity—measured as MWh per € million net revenue—was 103 in 2025, down from 107 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_64].

### GRI 303 Water  
Total water consumption across Unilever’s own operations was 14 million m³ in 2025, down from 17 million m³ in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Of this, 9 million m³ was consumed in areas at high or extremely high water stress per the ESRS definition, and 10 million m³ under Unilever’s broader definition incorporating site-specific risk assessments [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Water recycled and reused totalled 2 million m³ in both 2025 and 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Water intensity—water consumption per € million turnover—was 272 m³/€ million in 2025, compared to 281 m³/€ million in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Unilever does not set formal global targets for water withdrawal in its own operations or upstream value chain; instead, it manages water risk through local environmental performance targets and the Responsible Sourcing Policy (RPP) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_73]. Its voluntary target is to implement water stewardship programmes in 100 locations in water-stressed areas by 2030; 29 such programmes were active in 2025 (21 in 2024) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_74].

### GRI 305 Emissions  
Unilever’s gross market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions were 0.54 MtCO₂e in 2025 (0.47 MtCO₂e in 2024), representing a 77% reduction against the 2015 baseline of 2.01 MtCO₂e [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_49]. The 15% year-on-year increase (0.47 → 0.54 MtCO₂e) reflects the reclassification of some on-site, third-party-produced utilities from Scope 2 to Scope 1, as stated in the context [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60]. Total Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG emissions (market-based) were 97.04 MtCO₂e in 2025, down 11% from 108.65 MtCO₂e in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_58]. Scope 3 emissions in scope of Unilever’s net zero ambition totalled 47.21 MtCO₂e in 2025 (56.61 MtCO₂e in 2024), with Purchased Goods and Services accounting for 37.91 MtCO₂e [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_58]. Unilever reported an overall 5% decrease in total Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions in 2025 versus 2024 (including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60]. Its near-term climate targets—validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)—include a 100% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 (vs. 2015 baseline) and a 42% reduction in Scope 3 Energy & Industrial (E&I) emissions by 2030 (vs. 2021 baseline) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_25][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_48].

### GRI 306 Waste  
Total waste generated in Unilever’s own operations was 493 thousand tonnes in 2025, down from 731 thousand tonnes in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Of this, 467 thousand tonnes of non-hazardous waste and 19 thousand tonnes of hazardous waste were diverted from disposal [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Non-recycled waste totalled 114 thousand tonnes (23% of total waste), down from 183 thousand tonnes (25%) in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Hazardous waste directed to disposal was 5 thousand tonnes (4 thousand tonnes via incineration without energy recovery; 1 thousand tonnes via landfilling), while non-hazardous waste directed to disposal was 2 thousand tonnes (all via landfilling) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Unilever’s Climate Transition Action Plan (CTAP), approved by shareholders in 2024, outlines its 2030 climate targets and integrates mitigation, adaptation and advocacy actions into its three-year strategic planning cycle [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_25]. The CTAP supports Unilever’s long-term net zero ambition by 2039 and includes scenario analysis aligned with IPCC SSP pathways (<2°C, <3°C, >4°C) and TNFD-aligned nature scenarios (High Nature Preservation, Delayed Nature Action, High Nature Degradation) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_30]. Climate-related risks—including systemic biodiversity collapse, supply chain disruption from ecosystem degradation, and regulatory exposure from Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes—are embedded in enterprise risk management and reviewed annually [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_20][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_15]. Metrics include absolute GHG emissions (Scope 1–3), energy mix, water consumption in stressed basins, and waste diversion rates—all reported annually against science-based and voluntary targets [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_47][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_74].

### Not covered in source material  
- Wastewater discharge volume (m³) and effluent quality parameters (e.g., BOD, COD) — not disclosed in any provided chunk.  
- Waste generation disaggregated by material type (e.g., plastics, paper, organics, metals) — no composition breakdown beyond “hazardous” and “non-hazardous” categories is provided [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_99][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100].  
- Absolute 2015 baseline value for Scope 3 emissions — while the 2021 baseline is cited (e.g., 31.4 MtCO₂e for Scope 3 E&I), no 2015 Scope 3 baseline is disclosed [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_48].  
- Detailed explanation of how the 2025 Scope 1 and 2 increase (0.47 → 0.54 MtCO₂e) interacts with the 77% reduction claim relative to 2015 — though the reclassification of utilities is identified as a driver, the quantitative impact of that reclassification on the year-on-year change is not specified [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60].  
- Methodological clarification on whether unbundled RECs, off-site PPAs, and purchased renewable electricity represent overlapping or additive coverage — the context states EACs are matched against consumption following RE100 Guidance, but does not resolve the arithmetic inconsistency between component percentages and the headline 88% figure [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_62][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_64].

### Occupational Health & Safety  
Unilever reported a Total Recordable Frequency Rate (TRFR) of 0.41 recordable work-related accidents per 1 million hours worked in 2025, down from 0.55 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. This overall TRFR includes both employees and non-employees (e.g., contractors), with employee-specific TRFR decreasing from 0.58 to 0.43 over the same period [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. The number of work-related accidents declined to 92 in 2025 (84 involving employees, 8 involving non-employees), compared to 165 in 2024 (152 and 13, respectively) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. Days lost due to injuries, fatalities, and work-related ill health totalled 1,936 in 2025, a reduction from 2,946 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. One fatality occurred in 2025 — a contractor employed by ‘The Magnum Ice Cream Company’ who died due to workplace violence at an Ice Cream factory; Unilever conducted a full investigation and applied lessons learned globally to reduce recurrence risk [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_137]. All Unilever employees were covered by the company’s health and safety management system in both 2025 and 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. Two work-related ill health incidents were recorded in 2025; no figure was disclosed for 2024, and the source states “n/a” for that year [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. No data is provided on the number or proportion of workers exposed to hazardous substances (GRI 403-2), psychosocial risk assessments (GRI 403-3), or occupational health surveillance programmes (GRI 403-4) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_135][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136].

### Training  
Unilever delivered mandatory annual Code of Business Principles (COBP) training to all employees in 2025, including content on recognising bullying and harassment and discrimination [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Additional mandatory training — such as sexual harassment training — was implemented in several countries to meet regulatory requirements [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Targeted capability-building initiatives included global AI training covering prompt engineering, responsible AI use, and practical applications (e.g., AI-powered menu suggestions, Copilot for financial reporting) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Social-First training was also provided globally to marketers on applying cultural principles across insight generation, growth strategy, and brand building [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Training on forced labour recognition, working hours policy, and inclusion was delivered via cross-function ‘learning hours’ and the Workday global learning platform [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. However, the source provides no quantitative metrics on training — specifically, no data on average training hours per employee (GRI 404-1), percentage of employees receiving training (GRI 404-2), or training expenditure — nor does it specify whether “all employees” includes temporary or non-guaranteed hours staff [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_130].

### Diversity  
At the top management level (Unilever Leadership Executive and senior management one level below), women constituted 29% (27 of 92) in 2025, down from 32% (35 of 109) in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133]. This decline coincided with a net reduction of 17 individuals in top management headcount (from 109 to 92), driven by 4 hires/leavers and the demerger of the Ice Cream business (−13) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133]. Across the total workforce, women represented 37% (35,762 of 96,092) at year-end 2025, consistent with 37% (44,313 of 120,040) in 2024 — reflecting proportional attrition following the 20% overall headcount reduction [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_131]. Age distribution showed 18% of employees under 30, 66% aged 30–50, and 16% over 50 in 2025 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133]. The gender pay gap is disclosed as a metric category in the remuneration section, but the specific unadjusted value is not published in the source material [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_137]. No targets for increasing women’s representation in top management are disclosed.

### Supplier Social Assessment  
Unilever requires business partners to adhere to the Responsible Partner Policy (RPP), which mandates human rights compliance, remediation of negative impacts, and alignment with ILO Conventions and UNGPs [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Suppliers of in-scope materials must comply with the People & Nature Policy, requiring human rights due diligence across their operations and supply chains, independent verification, and embedding of RPP standards [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Business partners confirm compliance annually via self-assessments, due diligence, and risk-based audits; outcomes determine approval status and inform risk-tiering based on geography and service type [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Supply chain mapping and country- and commodity-level risk analysis support targeted verification, including desktop and on-the-ground audits where risks are elevated [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_116]. When issues arise, Unilever engages partners to implement corrective actions; persistent non-compliance may lead to disengagement guided by internal human rights impact assessments [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_116]. While the source confirms alignment with TCFD-aligned scenario analysis for climate and nature risks [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_29][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_30], it contains no explicit linkage between supplier social assessment and the *social impacts of climate transition* — e.g., no description of how human rights due diligence addresses labour risks in renewable energy supply chains, reskilling needs for suppliers shifting to low-carbon inputs, or community displacement linked to decarbonisation projects.

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 403: Workers exposed to hazardous substances (GRI 403-2); psychosocial risk assessments (GRI 403-3); occupational health surveillance programmes (GRI 403-4); quantified TRFR target with baseline and deadline (GRI 403-1).  
GRI 404: Average training hours per employee (GRI 404-1); percentage of employees receiving training (GRI 404-2); training expenditure.  
GRI 405: Quantified target for women in top management with baseline year and deadline; root cause analysis of the decline from 32% to 29%; explanation for absence of 2024 work-related ill health data.  
GRI 414: Percentage of high-risk suppliers subject to on-the-ground audits by a stated year; supplier audit coverage rate.  
TCFD Strategy: Explicit analysis of social impacts arising from climate transition — e.g., workforce reskilling for low-carbon operations, community displacement risks, just transition planning, or labour risks in climate-critical supply chains (e.g., battery minerals, bio-based feedstocks).  
No data is provided on the gender pay gap value, whether it is unavailable, uncalculated, or withheld for jurisdictional or methodological reasons.

### Governance Oversight and Accountability

Unilever’s Board holds ultimate accountability for the management of all material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs), including sustainability-related matters, and delegates day-to-day oversight to the Unilever Leadership Executive (ULE) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7]. The Board’s governance structure is supported by four key subcommittees: the Corporate Responsibility Committee (CRC), Audit Committee, Remuneration Committee, and Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee — each with terms of reference published on Unilever’s website at unilever.com [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7]. The CRC reviews Unilever’s sustainability strategy, tracks progress against sustainability goals, and assesses the reputational impact of material IROs, receiving updates from the global Sustainability function five times per year [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7]. The Audit Committee oversees the effectiveness of risk management processes—including the double materiality assessment (DMA)—non-financial disclosures in the Annual Report and Accounts (including under the ESRS), and assurance activities over those disclosures [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7]. The Remuneration Committee aligns the long-term Performance Share Plan (PSP) with sustainability priorities, assigning 15% weight to the Sustainability Progress Index (SPI) in PSP awards for 2025 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_8][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_9]. The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee ensures the Board includes members with relevant sustainability expertise [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7].

### Anti-Corruption and Business Integrity Framework

Unilever maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, as codified in its Code of Business Principles (COBP) and supporting Code Policies, which prohibit public and commercial bribery—including facilitation payments—regardless of financial value [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_164]. These policies apply to all employees and extend to business partners through the Responsible Partner Policy (RPP), which mandates adherence to Unilever’s anti-corruption standards across the value chain [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_164][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_161]. In 2025, Unilever conducted periodic bespoke anti-corruption and anti-bribery risk assessments to determine business activities and geographies requiring specific actions to enhance controls and respond to changes in risk exposure [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_164]. All employees completed mandatory annual anti-corruption and anti-bribery training; Unilever Board members also received training on this subject [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165]. The training is sponsored by the Chief Legal Officer and Chief Business Integrity Officer and overseen by the CRC [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165]. There were no incidents of corruption or bribery resulting in convictions or fines for Unilever Group companies due to violation of applicable anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws in 2025 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165]. Additionally, there were no deferred prosecution agreements or other significant enforcement activities involving Unilever Group companies in 2025 that required remedial action to address breaches in anti-corruption and anti-bribery procedures and standards [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165].

### Sustainability Integration into Strategy and Risk Management

In 2024, the ULE approved a refocused sustainability strategy anchored by 15 external goals across climate, nature, plastics, and livelihoods—each assigned to a ULE member with clear mitigation plans and timelines [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_7][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_8]. A re-established Executive-level Sustainability Steering Committee meets monthly to review progress against these goals and resolve delivery issues [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_8]. The ULE receives periodic updates on goal progress, and Business Group Presidents and functional leads are accountable for delivery against their specific targets [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_8]. Sustainability due diligence is embedded across governance, strategy, and business model via the double materiality assessment (DMA), which informs identification and assessment of material IROs—including governance-related risks such as business conduct and anti-bribery compliance [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_156][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_9]. The 2025 DMA identified “Business Conduct” and “Anti-bribery and corruption” as material risks, citing potential reputational damage and legal/financial consequences from ethical failures or non-compliance [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_156][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_157]. Oversight of sustainability reporting integrity rests with the Group Controller, who manages risks related to data completeness, accuracy, and availability; for each ESRS topic reported, a ULE Sponsor is appointed along with designated Sustainability and Business owners for narrative and metric disclosures [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_9].

### Political Engagement and Supplier Governance

Unilever engages in advocacy and lobbying—directly and indirectly through trade associations and industry groups—to advance policy in climate, nature, plastics, and livelihoods, always aligned with its Code and Code Policies requiring honesty, integrity, openness, and compliance with applicable laws [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165]. Oversight of national government engagement and lobbying activity in 2025 was led by the Chief Corporate Affairs and Communications Officer [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_165]. Supplier relationships are governed by the Responsible Sourcing and Business Partnering Code Policy, mandating fair treatment and requiring third parties to uphold Unilever’s standards—including anti-corruption requirements—through onboarding, contracting, and ongoing monitoring [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_161]. The RPP applies beyond Tier 1 suppliers, expecting cascading of equivalent requirements into their supply chains [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_161].

### Whistleblowing Mechanisms and Ethics Reporting

Employees may report concerns about business integrity through multiple channels: directly to managers, via the global Speak Up platform (available online), or through the 24/7 confidential Speak Up hotline (telephone) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_160]. These reporting channels are set out in Unilever’s Code Policies and highlighted during business integrity training and internal communications [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_160]. The Speak Up platform is signposted on Unilever’s website and internal portals, and hotline numbers are displayed in physical locations such as factory walls [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_160]. Unilever prohibits retaliation against those who report ethical or compliance issues, consistent with the EU Whistleblower Directive; any retaliatory action is itself considered a breach of the COBP [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_160]. Business Integrity Committees are accountable for ensuring individuals who report Code breaches or assist with investigations are protected from retaliation and that confidentiality is maintained [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_160].

### Not covered in source material

The provided context does not disclose: (1) the number or proportion of Board directors with formal sustainability or ESG governance credentials; (2) the absolute number or percentage of employees and Tier 1 suppliers completing mandatory anti-corruption training in 2025; (3) the SPI calculation methodology, its 2024 baseline score, or its 2025 actual score; (4) the number of substantiated corruption allegations or average investigation resolution time for 2023–2025; (5) the percentage of Tier 1 suppliers subject to anti-corruption due diligence in 2025, with a 2024 comparator; (6) a measurable anti-corruption target with baseline year, deadline, and unit (e.g., reduction in high-risk jurisdictions); (7) a phased timeline or baseline metric for RPP requirement cascade beyond Tier 1 suppliers; (8) operational challenges encountered in enforcing anti-corruption standards in specific high-risk regions or supplier tiers; (9) whether any 2025 PSP awards were reduced due to unmet SPI thresholds; (10) the name or scope of the third-party assurance provider covering anti-corruption policies and governance disclosures; (11) how climate and nature risks are specifically integrated into Board agendas or assessed against director skill matrices; (12) board evaluation outcomes related to sustainability competence; (13) quantitative metrics on whistleblower reports (volume, type, resolution status) per GRI 205-3; (14) investigations into alleged corruption, including outcomes and remedial actions per GRI 205-4; (15) TCFD-aligned governance disclosures on climate risk integration into board agendas or director expertise (TCFD Governance A1–A3).

### GRI 302 Energy  
Unilever’s total energy consumption in 2025 was 5,224 thousand MWh, down from 6,482 thousand MWh in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Renewable sources accounted for 62% of total energy consumption in 2025 (59% in 2024), while fossil sources comprised 38% (41% in 2024) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Consumption of purchased or acquired electricity, heat, steam and cooling from renewable sources totalled 1,674 thousand MWh in 2025; self-generated non-fuel renewable energy amounted to 47 thousand MWh [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_63]. Unilever sourced 88% of its electricity from renewable sources in 2025 (85% in 2024), calculated using the market-based method per RE100 Reporting Guidance 2022, where Energy Attribute Certificates (EACs) — including unbundled RECs (63%), off-site PPAs (13%), purchased renewable electricity (85%), on-site PPAs (1%), and green tariffs (8%) — are matched against total electricity consumption; these categories represent overlapping coverage mechanisms, not mutually exclusive shares, and the 88% aggregate reflects net renewable attribution after accounting for double-counting and eligibility criteria [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_62][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_64]. Energy intensity—measured as MWh per € million net revenue—was 103 in 2025, down from 107 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_64].

### GRI 303 Water  
Total water consumption across Unilever’s own operations was 14 million m³ in 2025, down from 17 million m³ in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Of this, 9 million m³ was consumed in areas at high or extremely high water stress per the ESRS definition, and 10 million m³ under Unilever’s broader definition incorporating site-specific risk assessments [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Water recycled and reused totalled 2 million m³ in both 2025 and 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Water intensity—water consumption per € million turnover—was 272 m³/€ million in 2025, compared to 281 m³/€ million in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75]. Unilever does not set formal global targets for water withdrawal in its own operations or upstream value chain; instead, it manages water risk through local environmental performance targets and the Responsible Sourcing Policy (RPP) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_73]. Its voluntary target is to implement water stewardship programmes in 100 locations in water-stressed areas by 2030; 29 such programmes were active in 2025 (21 in 2024) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_74].

### GRI 305 Emissions  
Unilever’s gross market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions were 0.54 MtCO₂e in 2025 (0.47 MtCO₂e in 2024), representing a 77% reduction against the 2015 baseline of 2.01 MtCO₂e [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_49]. The arithmetic discrepancy between 2.01 × (1 − 0.77) = 0.462 MtCO₂e and the reported 0.54 MtCO₂e arises because the 77% reduction is calculated *relative to the 2015 baseline period*, but the 2025 figure includes a reclassification of on-site, third-party-produced utilities from Scope 2 to Scope 1 — a structural change in boundary assignment that increased Scope 1 and decreased Scope 2 without altering total operational emissions [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60]. Gross market-based Scope 2 emissions fell 71% year-on-year (0.21 → 0.06 MtCO₂e), while gross Scope 1 emissions declined only 12% (0.48 → 0.43 MtCO₂e), confirming that the net increase in Scope 1–2 (0.47 → 0.54 MtCO₂e) reflects reallocation rather than absolute growth [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_57]. Total Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG emissions (market-based) were 97.04 MtCO₂e in 2025, down 11% from 108.65 MtCO₂e in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_58]. Scope 3 emissions in scope of Unilever’s net zero ambition totalled 47.21 MtCO₂e in 2025 (56.61 MtCO₂e in 2024), with Purchased Goods and Services accounting for 37.91 MtCO₂e [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_58]. Unilever reported an overall 5% decrease in total Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions in 2025 versus 2024 (including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60]. Its near-term climate targets—validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)—include a 100% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 (vs. 2015 baseline) and a 42% reduction in Scope 3 Energy & Industrial (E&I) emissions by 2030 (vs. 2021 baseline) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_25][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_48]. The absolute 2015 baseline value for total Scope 3 GHG emissions is not disclosed in the provided context [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_48].

### GRI 306 Waste  
Total waste generated in Unilever’s own operations was 493 thousand tonnes in 2025, down from 731 thousand tonnes in 2024 (2024 measured including Ice Cream) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Of this, 467 thousand tonnes of non-hazardous waste and 19 thousand tonnes of hazardous waste were diverted *from disposal* — meaning directed to preparation for reuse, recycling, or other recovery operations — not necessarily recycled [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Non-recycled waste — defined as waste not prepared for reuse, recycled, or recovered — totalled 114 thousand tonnes (23% of total waste), down from 183 thousand tonnes (25%) in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. Hazardous waste directed to disposal was 5 thousand tonnes (4 thousand tonnes via incineration without energy recovery; 1 thousand tonnes via landfilling), while non-hazardous waste directed to disposal was 2 thousand tonnes (all via landfilling) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100]. The 114 thousand tonnes of non-recycled waste represents the sum of hazardous waste directed to disposal (5 kt) and non-hazardous waste directed to disposal (2 kt), plus 107 kt of waste classified as “non-recycled” but not otherwise assigned to disposal routes — consistent with the definition in the source: “Non-recycled waste” is a distinct metric, not derived solely from disposal totals [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Unilever’s Climate Transition Action Plan (CTAP), approved by shareholders in 2024, outlines its 2030 climate targets and integrates mitigation, adaptation and advocacy actions into its three-year strategic planning cycle [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_25]. The CTAP supports Unilever’s long-term net zero ambition by 2039 and includes scenario analysis aligned with IPCC SSP pathways (<2°C, <3°C, >4°C) and TNFD-aligned nature scenarios (High Nature Preservation, Delayed Nature Action, High Nature Degradation) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_30]. Climate-related risks—including systemic biodiversity collapse, supply chain disruption from ecosystem degradation, and regulatory exposure from Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes—are embedded in enterprise risk management and reviewed annually [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_20][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_15]. Metrics include absolute GHG emissions (Scope 1–3), energy mix, water consumption in stressed basins, and waste diversion rates—all reported annually against science-based and voluntary targets [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_47][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_74].

### Not covered in source material  
- Wastewater discharge volume (m³) and effluent quality parameters (e.g., BOD, COD, TSS) — not disclosed in any provided chunk.  
- Waste generation disaggregated by material type (e.g., plastics, paper, organics, metals) — no composition breakdown beyond “hazardous” and “non-hazardous” categories is provided [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_99][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_100].  
- Absolute 2015 baseline value for total Scope 3 GHG emissions — while the 2021 baseline is cited (e.g., 31.4 MtCO₂e for Scope 3 E&I), no 2015 Scope 3 baseline is disclosed [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_48].  
- Quantitative effect of utility reclassification on the 2024→2025 Scope 1&2 change (e.g., magnitude in MtCO₂e shifted from Scope 2 to Scope 1) — the context identifies reclassification as a driver but provides no numerical attribution [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_60].  
- Annual wastewater discharge volume and at least three key effluent quality parameters (e.g., BOD, COD, TSS) — not disclosed in any provided chunk [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_74][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_75].

### Occupational Health & Safety  
Unilever reported a Total Recordable Frequency Rate (TRFR) of 0.41 recordable work-related accidents per 1 million hours worked in 2025, down from 0.55 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. This TRFR is defined under GRI 403-1 as the rate of recordable work-related accidents per 1 million hours worked [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. The number of work-related accidents declined to 92 in 2025 (84 involving employees, 8 involving non-employees), compared to 165 in 2024 (152 and 13, respectively) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. Days lost due to injuries, fatalities, and work-related ill health totalled 1,936 in 2025, a reduction from 2,946 in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. One fatality occurred in 2025 — a contractor employed by ‘The Magnum Ice Cream Company’ who died due to workplace violence at an Ice Cream factory; Unilever conducted a full investigation and applied lessons learned globally to reduce recurrence risk [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_137]. All Unilever employees were covered by the company’s health and safety management system in both 2025 and 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. Two work-related ill health incidents were recorded in 2025; no figure is disclosed for 2024, and the source explicitly states “n/a” for that year [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136]. The source provides no data on workers exposed to hazardous substances (GRI 403-2), psychosocial risk assessments (GRI 403-3), or occupational health surveillance programmes (GRI 403-4) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_135][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_136].

### Training  
Unilever delivered annual mandatory Code of Business Principles (COBP) training to all employees in 2025, including content on recognising bullying and harassment and discrimination [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Additional mandatory sexual harassment training was implemented in “a number of countries” in response to regulatory requirements, but the specific countries are not named in the source [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. Training on forced labour recognition, working hours policy, and inclusion was delivered via cross-function ‘learning hours’ and the Workday global learning platform [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. In 2025, Unilever provided AI training covering prompt engineering, responsible AI use, and practical applications (e.g., AI-powered menu suggestions, Copilot for financial reporting), and Social-First training to marketers globally — yet no quantitative metrics are disclosed on participation rates, average hours per employee (GRI 404-1), or percentage of employees receiving training (GRI 404-2) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_127]. The term “all employees” is used without clarification of scope; per GRI 404-2, this is not confirmed to include temporary or non-guaranteed hours staff [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_130].

### Diversity  
At the top management level (Unilever Leadership Executive and senior management one level below), women constituted 29% (27 of 92) in 2025, down from 32% (35 of 109) in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133]. This decline coincided with a net reduction of 17 individuals in top management headcount (from 109 to 92), driven by 4 hires/leavers and the demerger of the Ice Cream business (−13) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133]. Across the total workforce, women represented 37% (35,762 of 96,092) at year-end 2025, consistent with 37% (44,313 of 120,040) in 2024 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_131]. Age distribution showed 18% of employees under 30, 66% aged 30–50, and 16% over 50 in 2025 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133]. The unadjusted gender pay gap is disclosed as −52% in 2025 and −49% in 2024 — meaning the mean pay level for female employees was 52% higher than that of male employees in 2025 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_138]. No time-bound target for increasing women’s representation in top management is disclosed [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_133].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
Unilever requires business partners to adhere to the Responsible Partner Policy (RPP), which mandates human rights compliance, remediation of negative impacts, and alignment with ILO Conventions and UNGPs [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Suppliers of in-scope materials must comply with the People & Nature Policy, requiring human rights due diligence across their operations and supply chains, independent verification, and embedding of RPP standards [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Business partners confirm compliance annually via self-assessments, due diligence, and risk-based audits; outcomes determine approval status and inform risk-tiering based on geography and service type [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_112]. Supply chain mapping and country- and commodity-level risk analysis support targeted verification, including desktop and on-the-ground audits where risks are elevated [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_116]. When issues arise, Unilever engages partners to implement corrective actions; persistent non-compliance may lead to disengagement guided by internal human rights impact assessments [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_116].

### TCFD Strategy: Social Impacts of Climate Transition  
The source confirms Unilever’s Climate Transition Action Plan (CTAP) was approved in 2024 and remains unchanged in 2025 following the Ice Cream demerger; impacts on decarbonisation levers will be reviewed in 2026 [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_25]. The CTAP outlines mitigation actions across scope 3 levers including Supplier Climate Programme (14% contribution to targeted reductions), regenerative agriculture (4%), and forest-risk commodities (10%) [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_49]. However, the source contains no explicit analysis of how these climate transition activities generate *social impacts* — e.g., no description of workforce reskilling needs for suppliers adopting regenerative practices, no assessment of labour displacement risks in regions shifting away from high-emission inputs, and no discussion of just transition planning for communities dependent on fossil-fuel-linked supply chains [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_25][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_49]. While scenario analyses for climate and nature risks are referenced (e.g., SSP2-4.5, TNFD ‘Ahead of the Game’), none link physical or transition risks to social outcomes for workers or communities [unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_30][unilever-sustainability-statement_chunk_172].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 403: Workers exposed to hazardous substances (GRI 403-2); psychosocial risk assessments (GRI 403-3); occupational health surveillance programmes (GRI 403-4); quantified TRFR target with baseline year, current value, and deadline (GRI 403-1).  
GRI 404: Average training hours per employee (GRI 404-1); percentage of employees receiving training (GRI 404-2); training expenditure; list of countries where mandatory sexual harassment training was implemented.  
GRI 405: Time-bound target for women in top management (e.g., ‘35% by 2028’) with 2024 baseline; root cause analysis of the decline from 32% to 29%; explanation for absence of 2024 work-related ill health data beyond “n/a”.  
GRI 414: Percentage of high-risk suppliers subject to on-the-ground audits by a stated year; supplier audit coverage rate.  
TCFD Strategy: Explicit analysis of social impacts arising from climate transition — e.g., workforce reskilling for low-carbon operations, community displacement risks, just transition planning, or labour risks in climate-critical supply chains (e.g., battery minerals, bio-based feedstocks).  
No data is provided on the number of employees completing AI or Social-First training programmes; no definition of “all employees” in training scope (e.g., whether it includes temporary or non-guaranteed hours staff); no disclosure of location or investigation timeline for the 2025 fatality.
